blocks.text: Hi, I'm L_404. I work in ISP technical support in the Philippines, and in my spare time I learn cybersecurity in legal labs: TryHackMe, HackTheBox, DVWA and CTFs.

My goal is to build real coding fundamentals by writing C, C++, Python and scripting by hand. Strong enough to move into offensive security, with red teaming as the target. Learn the machine, then learn to break it.

items.label: Chapter 1 · Oct–Dec 2024
items.title: By hand
items.text: Learned Python by writing it myself, using AI only to ask questions. Basics and small games first, then a banking system: a console app, a GUI version, and my own bug report with fixes.

items.label: Chapter 2 · from Feb 2026
items.title: Building with AI agents
items.text: When AI agents and CLI tools arrived, I learned how to orchestrate them: planning the work, splitting it across agents, reviewing what they built and shipping it. I even built my own workspace app for it, GridSpace, where I've journaled every session since day one.

items.label: Chapter 3 · Oct 2026 →
items.title: Back to the fundamentals
items.text: Building with agents is one skill. Writing code yourself is another. So I'm back to writing code by hand, and every project is reviewed and scored. My 2024 work counts as my Python baseline.

blocks.text: I study offensive security, malware analysis and detection engineering. The way I learn is by building: I wrote two malware samples against virtual machines I own — a rough first one in Python, then a far more sophisticated one in C — took them apart, and wrote the detections that would catch them. The goal was never to write malware; it was to understand it well enough to defend against it.

Everything below was built, run and tested by me inside my own isolated lab — no real targets, no third parties. Every technique is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. The numbers below are the real count from each sample.

blocks.label: The journey · three phases
blocks.note: From a rough first build, to a native agent, to defending my own work.

items.label: Phase 1 · Python
items.title: Getting my hands dirty
items.text: My first builds, written to understand the basics: talking to the Windows API, how malware survives a reboot, hiding strings from static analysis, and polling a public page for commands instead of a live server. Rough on purpose — that was the point.

items.label: Phase 2 · C
items.title: Going native
items.text: A bigger native Windows agent with a full command-and-control channel. This is where the real learning was: Windows internals in depth, how and why attackers get past built-in defenses (so I'd know exactly where a defender should look), and working from a beginner's crypto mistake up to a proper key-exchange handshake.

items.label: Phase 3 · Detection
items.title: Defending my own work
items.text: The turning point: I started writing detections for the malware I'd written — static signatures, behaviour rules mapped to a SIEM, and hunt scripts for the artifacts I planted. Every evasion I built, I can now name the detection that would have caught it. This is the half I care about most.

items.label: Framework
items.title: Mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
items.text: I document every technique I study against the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Mapping each one to an ID forced me to think in tactics (what the attacker wants) versus techniques (how they get it) — the same model a SOC analyst uses.

items.label: My own setup
items.title: Home lab & hands-on practice
items.text: An isolated lab I built from scratch — a Kali attacker and Windows targets on their own network — plus TryHackMe rooms, PortSwigger web-security labs, and reverse engineering in Ghidra.
